capability_notes.analyze: SQLite has no EXPLAIN ANALYZE. It has EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN (no actual row counts) and nothing that reports measured per-node time, so M5's plan-reading chapter cannot exist in this dialect.
capability_notes.plan: The planner's output is a tree of scan and search steps, not a cost model: no estimated rows, no actual rows, no cost. Reporting costs would be invented, so plan:false.
capability_notes.roles: Authentication is the host's job; SQLite has no roles, no GRANT, and no per-user privileges. Queries that probe pg_roles have no counterpart.
capability_notes.schemas: There is one namespace and no search_path. Tables are unqualified; the PostgreSQL dataset schema has no SQLite equivalent.
capability_notes.writable: The file is the database and the engine writes to it. The read-only posture of an anonymous learner is enforced by the host (query_only / a read-only open), not by the engine's permission model.
capability_notes.sqlstate: SQLite has primary result codes such as SQLITE_CONSTRAINT(19), not five-character SQLSTATE values. Error classification is by message pattern and is tested per code.
capability_notes.explain_query_plan: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN returns one row per step as text; it is available and is the dialect's plan affordance, distinct from analyze.
capability_notes.window_functions: Present since 3.25; the same shapes (PARTITION BY, ORDER BY, frame) parse, with SQLite's own typing and ordering rules.
capability_notes.recursive_cte: WITH RECURSIVE is present; the M9 lesson shape has a SQLite counterpart.
capability_notes.returning: RETURNING is present since 3.35, so a writing exercise can see its own rows.
capability_notes.strict_tables: STRICT tables (3.37) enforce the declared type, but they are opt-in per table; this dataset does not use them, so declared types stay advisory.
capability_notes.right_full_join: RIGHT and FULL OUTER JOIN are present since 3.39; LEFT JOIN has always been.
capability_notes.json1: JSON functions are compiled in by default from 3.38; the SQLite dataset does not rely on them.
capability_notes.boolean_type: There is no BOOLEAN storage class. TRUE/FALSE are keywords for 1/0 (3.23+) and the domain is unenforced, so a boolean column is reported as an integer.
capability_notes.date_type: There is no DATE or TIMESTAMP storage class. A DATE declaration only picks NUMERIC affinity, and ISO-8601 text is not a numeric literal, so the value is stored as text.
capability_notes.interval_type: There is no INTERVAL type and no interval arithmetic; a duration is a count plus modifiers passed to date().
capability_notes.dynamic_typing: A value's type is a property of the value, not the column. The declared type names an affinity applied on write; afterwards a column may hold any of the five classes.
capability_notes.rowid_tables: Every ordinary table has a hidden rowid unless WITHOUT ROWID is declared; INTEGER PRIMARY KEY is an alias for it.
capability_notes.without_rowid: WITHOUT ROWID is available for a table keyed by its primary key. This dataset keeps rowid tables so the hidden id is a teaching point.
capability_notes.autoincrement: AUTOINCREMENT exists but is not the default and only changes INTEGER PRIMARY KEY reuse; this dataset supplies explicit ids, so no AUTOINCREMENT (and no sqlite_sequence table) is used. PostgreSQL's GENERATED ... IDENTITY has no SQLite counterpart.
capability_notes.like_case_insensitive_ascii: LIKE is case-insensitive for ASCII by default (ILIKE does not exist). The wrong habit — assuming LIKE is case-sensitive — is what the dialect must teach against.
capability_notes.ilike: No ILIKE. Case-insensitive matching is LIKE, or GLOB/UPPER for a case-sensitive or non-ASCII-precise comparison.
capability_notes.date_trunc: DATE_TRUNC does not exist. The dialect's date_trunc equivalent is strftime('%Y-%m-01', d) or date(d, 'start of month').
capability_notes.to_char: TO_CHAR does not exist; formatting is printf()/strftime().
capability_notes.distinct_on: DISTINCT ON does not exist; the equivalent is a window function or GROUP BY plus an aggregate.
capability_notes.cast_operator: The :: cast operator does not exist. CAST(x AS type) does, and its rules differ: SQLite's CAST follows SQLite's own affinity rules.
capability_notes.interrupt: sqlite3_interrupt stops a running statement, and SQLITE_INTERRUPT(9) is a reachable result code, so the host can honour a deadline.

types.note: A declared type in SQLite names an affinity, not a constraint. The first matching rule below decides the affinity; the order is SQLite's own, from https://sqlite.org/datatype3.html section 3.1.

affinity_rules.note: INTEGER, INT and BIGINT all land here. INTEGER PRIMARY KEY is also the rowid alias, which is the only identity mechanism this dataset needs.
TEXT, VARCHAR(20) and CHARACTER land here. TEXT affinity never converts a number into text on write, so a number stays a number in a TEXT column.

affinity_rules.when: the declared type contains "BLOB", or the column has no declared type
affinity_rules.note: No affinity is applied: any value is stored as given. An untyped column and a BLOB column behave the same way.
REAL, FLOAT and DOUBLE land here. An integral real is written as an integer on disk and read back as a float, so a REAL column always reports a number.

NUMERIC, DECIMAL(10,2), DATE, TIMESTAMP and BOOLEAN all land here. Numeric-looking text becomes INTEGER or REAL on write; non-numeric text (an ISO-8601 date) stays text. This is why a DATE column holds TEXT.

value_encoding.note: SQLite reports a value's storage class (NULL, INTEGER, REAL, TEXT, BLOB), never the declared type. This is the class -> JSON value map the adapter must use; the declared affinity of the column deliberately does not change it.

integer.rule: an INTEGER is a JSON number

big_int.note: Above 2^53-1 a JSON number cannot hold the value exactly, so it is a decimal string. Same rule web/src/api/pglite.ts already applies to PostgreSQL bigint, so the two dialects agree.

integer.note: SQLite integers are signed 64-bit; only those outside the JSON safe range become strings.

real.rule: a REAL is a JSON number

non_finite.note: SQLite stores NaN as NULL, so NaN is reported as null, which is the engine's own answer. Infinity has no JSON literal: reporting null would hide a value and reporting a number would fabricate one, so it is reported as the string "Infinity"/"-Infinity".

real.note: JSON has no non-finite numbers; the named rule above keeps the report honest instead of rounding Inf to something finite.

text.rule: a TEXT value is the string verbatim
text.note: No parsing on the way out: a stored date stays the same text, and a numeric-looking string in a TEXT column stays a string (it was not converted on write).

blob.rule: a BLOB is \x followed by lowercase hex
blob.note: Matches PostgreSQL bytea's text form and the \x convention in web/src/api/pglite.ts, so both dialects report binary the same way.

null.note: SQL NULL is not the empty string and not zero; it is reported as null and is never substituted.

boolean.rule: a BOOLEAN-declared column stores 0/1 and is reported as an integer
boolean.note: There is no boolean class. TRUE/FALSE are keywords for 1/0 and the domain is unenforced, so coercion to true/false would be an invention; report the integer.

date.rule: a DATE- or TIMESTAMP-declared column stores ISO-8601 text and is reported verbatim
date.note: Dates are not a type. The value's class is TEXT, so it is emitted as a string and never as a host Date object — a JS Date would reintroduce the timezone shift the adapter-parity audit found against PGlite. Both adapters report the stored text: the browser reads sqlite3_column_text, and the gateway's read path (backend/internal/engine/sqlite_raw.go) reads the storage class through the same raw API, so the declared type is a label and nothing is materialised on either side.

time.rule: a value handed to the encoder as a time.Time is formatted as RFC3339 in UTC
time.note: Neither adapter reaches this rule: both read paths report a column's storage class, so a DATE- or TIMESTAMP-declared column arrives as its stored TEXT under the `date` rule above. It answers for a driver value that is already a time.Time, where the stored text is gone; RFC3339 in UTC is then the least-lossy string form and keeps the value a string.

column_type_label.rule: the declared type verbatim when the column has one, otherwise the fallback label
column_type_label.note: A declared type is not the value's type: a DATE column labels DATE while its values are TEXT. Expressions (COUNT(*), price * 2) have no declared type and must be labelled "expression" rather than claim a type the engine never had.

error_classification.note: SQLITE_ERROR(1). The common form is 'near "X": syntax error'.
SQLITE_ERROR(1). An equals match, not a contains match, because the whole message is exactly this text.
SQLITE_ERROR(1). A prefix match because the offending token is appended to the message.
SQLITE_ERROR(1): 'unterminated string literal', 'unterminated /* comment'.

SQLITE_BUSY(5). Contention spends the learner's deadline, exactly as PostgreSQL's pool-saturation path already reports QUERY_TIMEOUT. Equals so the shorter SQLITE_LOCKED message is not swallowed by it.
SQLITE_LOCKED(6): 'database table is locked'. Same reasoning as SQLITE_BUSY(5); the message names the writer where SQLite gives one.
SQLITE_INTERRUPT(9). The host stopped the statement because the deadline passed, so this is a timeout and not a learner error.
SQLITE_CANTOPEN(14): the database file is missing or the host cannot open it.
SQLITE_NOTADB(26): the file exists but is not a SQLite database.
SQLITE_CORRUPT(11): the environment is damaged; a learner query cannot cause or fix this.
SQLITE_IOERR(10): the storage layer failed.
SQLITE_FULL(13): out of space, not a query error.
SQLITE_PERM(3): the host's file permissions, not SQLite's privilege model.
SQLITE_NOMEM(7): the host ran out of memory serving the query.
SQLITE_MISUSE(21), 'bad parameter or other API misuse': a host bug, not something a learner wrote.
SQLITE_MISUSE(21), 'library routine called out of sequence': the second message form of the same primary code.
SQLITE_TOOBIG(18). The engine's own size cap. The adapter's row and byte caps are separate host limits and are reported with the same code, with truncated set.
SQLITE_ERROR(1) raised after parsing: the statement is valid but names something that does not exist.
SQLITE_ERROR(1), same reason as 'no such table'. PostgreSQL reports the equivalent SQLSTATE 42703 as a runtime error too.
SQLITE_ERROR(1). Covers a misspelled function and a function this build does not have.
SQLITE_ERROR(1): a virtual table or extension module is not compiled in.
SQLITE_ERROR(1). SQLite names the column; the message is reported verbatim so the learner can see which one.

SQLITE_CONSTRAINT(19) and every extended subtype: 'UNIQUE constraint failed', 'NOT NULL constraint failed', 'CHECK constraint failed', 'FOREIGN KEY constraint failed', 'PRIMARY KEY constraint failed'. All are runtime errors, not syntax errors.
SQLITE_MISMATCH(20), e.g. inserting text into a STRICT table's INTEGER column. Dynamic typing means this is rare, which is why it needs its own entry rather than being left to the catch-all.
SQLITE_ERROR(1): 'misuse of aggregate function', 'misuse of window function'. A valid-looking statement that misuses a construct.

error_classification.pattern: attempt to write a readonly database
error_classification.note: SQLITE_READONLY(8). This is how the anonymous read-only dataset refuses a write (step 5), and it must be a runtime error rather than an environment fault.
SQLITE_AUTH(23): a host-installed authorizer refused the statement.
SQLITE_AUTH(23), the second message form of the same primary code.
SQLITE_RANGE(25): 'column index out of range', 'parameter index out of range'.
Catch-all: every remaining SQLITE_ERROR(1) message is a runtime error, the same default the PostgreSQL classifier uses. The empty pattern matches every message, so this rule must stay last.
